# ECON 0100 | Vignette C1 | Externalities

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

Hogsmeade has recently seen a surge in shops selling Glittering Gum, a candy that makes one’s words sparkle and glisten as one speaks. The Demand curve and Supply curve for Glittering Gum can be represented using the following relationships:

$$
D: P_b = 30 - \frac{1}{2} Q_d \qquad\qquad S: P_s = 6 + \frac{1}{4} Q_s
$$

After years of careful epidemiological analysis, a subcommittee of the Ministry tasked with improving the health and wellbeing of the wizarding community published a story in the Daily Profit establishing a link between the consumption of Glittering Gum and “Starlight Sneeze,” a condition where non-consumers start sneezing out harmless but bothersome glitter. The estimate in the story is that this condition carries an inconvenience cost of 6 Coins per unit of Glittering Gum to those in Hogsmeade. 

Use a graph and algebra to find equilibrium price, quantity, and DWL.

::: solution

Equilibrium Price $\hat{P}$: $14$ coins. Equilibrium Quantity $\hat{Q}$: $32$ pieces of gum. Efficient Quantity $Q^*$: $24$ pieces of gum. Deadweight Loss: $24$ coins.

![Glittering Gum market with the cost of the Starlight Sneeze](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every piece of gum chewed adds $6$ coins of Starlight Sneeze on top of the cost of making it, so marginal social cost is supply shifted up by $6$:

$$
MSC: P = \left(6 + \tfrac{1}{4} Q\right) + 6 = 12 + \tfrac{1}{4} Q
$$

Buyers and sellers do not pay for the sneezing, so the market settles where demand meets supply:

$$
30 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 6 + \tfrac{1}{4} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad \tfrac{3}{4} Q = 24 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 32, \quad P = 30 - 16 = 14
$$

The efficient quantity counts the sneezing, so it sits where demand meets marginal social cost:

$$
30 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 12 + \tfrac{1}{4} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad \tfrac{3}{4} Q = 18 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 24, \quad P = 30 - 12 = 18
$$

The market makes $8$ pieces of gum too many. Each of the $25$th through $32$nd pieces is worth more to its buyer than it costs its seller, so it trades, but it is worth less than it costs society once the sneezing is counted. The $32$nd, for example, is worth $14$ to its buyer and costs society $12 + 8 = 20$. The losses on those pieces add up to the triangle between marginal social cost and demand from $24$ to $32$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (20 - 14) \times (32 - 24) = 24
$$

:::
